text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementHealthThere’s a New, International Food Pyramid in TownIt’s based on research into dietary guidelines from around the worldJCBy Jake Currie3:00 PM CDT on October 27, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleOur country has a long and tortured history with food pyramids. The original dietary schematic, unveiled in 1992, had a firm foundation of carbohydrates—the bread, cereals, rice, and pasta group. It may seem unimaginable now, but the federal government recommended getting a whopping 6 to 11 servings of these every day. Of course, those guidelines were dramatically revamped in 2011 when USDA officials ditched the pyramid shape altogether in favor of a simpler (and frankly more appropriate) plate design emphasizing grains, vegetables, and fruits and minimizing dairy.Then Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. came along, scrapped the plate, and inexplicably turned the pyramid upside down. His new inverted food pyramid has a base (on the top) consisting of protein, dairy, fats, vegetables, and fruit with an apex (on the bottom) made of whole grains. The two-front war on proteins and saturated fats was over, Kennedy declared, but a new war on sugar has begun. The U.S. government’s current inverted food pyramid.
